title: Herb Scissors for Kids: Supervised Projects with Multi‑Blade
meta_description: Teach your little chefs how to prep greens safely! Explore herb scissors kids supervised projects and the best ways to use multi-blade shears.
html:
There is something uniquely satisfying about a multi-blade shear. Watching a bunch of fresh basil transform into a fine mince in a single snip is a bit of kitchen magic. For parents, it’s also a great way to introduce children to food prep without the intimidation of a heavy chef's knife. When you set up herb scissors kids supervised projects, you're not just making dinner; you're teaching fine motor skills and culinary confidence.

The tool of choice for these activities is the Herb Scissors. These five-blade herb shears that mince cilantro, chives, and basil in one snip—complete with a cleaning comb—are designed for efficiency. Because they cut multiple strands at once, the process is faster, and the blades are easier to manage than a traditional knife for a child under close supervision.

Setting Up Your Herb Scissors Kids Supervised Projects

Before bringing the kids into the kitchen, set the stage for success. I recommend creating a "prep station" on a sturdy cutting board or a large baking sheet. This contains the clippings and gives the child a clear boundary for where the tool should be used.

Start with "soft" herbs. Cilantro, parsley, and chives are ideal because they don't require much pressure to cut. Show your child how to hold the handle firmly and how to snip in a rhythmic motion. Emphasize the "safety zone"—keeping fingers far away from the five blades at all times.

3 Easy Recipes for Little Helpers

To make these activities feel like a project rather than a chore, give the kids a specific goal. Here are three ways to use the Herb Scissors to create a finished dish:

  • The Green Topper: Have your child mince a mix of parsley and chives to sprinkle over a homemade potato soup or a bowl of steamed carrots.
  • Herb Butter Swirls: Soften a stick of salted butter. Let the kids mince fresh basil and a pinch of salt, then stir it into the butter for a fancy spread.
  • Fresh Pesto Pasta: While you handle the food processor for the nuts and cheese, let the kids use the multi-blade shears to prep the basil leaves for the base.

Safety Tips for Multi-Blade Shears

While these shears are more intuitive than a knife, they are still sharp tools. Supervision is non-negotiable. I always tell my kids that the scissors are "tools, not toys," and they stay on the counter until it's time to work.

One practical tip: teach children to cut "away" from their bodies. Instead of pulling the herbs toward their chest, they should snip forward or downward toward the board. This simple adjustment significantly reduces the risk of accidental nicks if the shears slip.

Cleaning Up with the Cleaning Comb

The biggest headache with multi-blade scissors is the buildup of herb residue between the blades. This is where the cleaning comb included with the Herb Scissors becomes a game-changer. It allows you to clear out the stubborn bits of cilantro or basil without putting your fingers directly between the sharp edges.

Turn the cleaning process into part of the lesson. Show your children how to use the comb to clear the blades, then rinse them under warm water. Teaching them that the job isn't done until the tool is clean is a habit that will save you hours of cleanup in the long run.

Choosing the Right Herbs for Kids

Not all greens are created equal. For the best results with supervised projects, stick to herbs with thin or tender stems. Basil, mint, and chives are the "gold standard" for five-blade shears. They slice cleanly and instantly.

Avoid woody stems, like those found on old rosemary or thick thyme branches. These can jam the blades or require too much force, which can cause a child's hand to slip. If you want to use rosemary, strip the needles off the stem first and let the kids snip just the needles.

FAQ

Are herb scissors safer than knives for children?

While no sharp tool is "safe," multi-blade shears are often less intimidating and easier to control than a chef's knife. They eliminate the need for a rocking motion or complex chopping techniques, making them a great entry point for supervised kitchen help.

How do I prevent the blades from sticking?

Use the provided cleaning comb after every session. If the blades feel sticky, a quick rinse with warm, soapy water and a thorough dry will prevent residue from hardening, ensuring the shears glide through the herbs easily.

Can children use these for other things, like scallions?

Yes! Green onions (scallions) are perfect for the Herb Scissors. They provide a great visual result and are a fantastic way to let kids help with salad or taco toppings.
